claim: The Par complex dynamically polarizes to the apical cortex of asymmetrically dividing Drosophila neuroblasts where it directs fate determinant segregation.
source: The Par complex dynamically polarizes to the apical cortex of asymmetrically dividing Drosophila neuroblasts where it directs fate determinant segregation.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about Par complex function in neuroblasts, serving as background for the study.

claim: Apically directed cortical movements that polarize the Par complex require F-actin.
source: Previously, we showed that apically directed cortical movements that polarize the Par complex require F-actin (Oon and Prehoda, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Cortical actomyosin dynamics begin in interphase when the Par complex is cytoplasmic.
source: Here, we report the discovery of cortical actomyosin dynamics that begin in interphase when the Par complex is cytoplasmic but ultimately become tightly coupled to cortical Par dynamics.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the current study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cortical actomyosin dynamics ultimately become tightly coupled to cortical Par dynamics.
source: Here, we report the discovery of cortical actomyosin dynamics that begin in interphase when the Par complex is cytoplasmic but ultimately become tightly coupled to cortical Par dynamics.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2 and Video 2.

claim: Interphase cortical actomyosin dynamics are unoriented and pulsatile.
source: Interphase cortical actomyosin dynamics are unoriented and pulsatile but rapidly become sustained and apically-directed in early mitosis when the Par protein aPKC accumulates on the cortex.
evidence: This characterization is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1 and Video 1.

claim: Cortical actomyosin dynamics rapidly become sustained and apically-directed in early mitosis when the Par protein aPKC accumulates on the cortex.
source: Interphase cortical actomyosin dynamics are unoriented and pulsatile but rapidly become sustained and apically-directed in early mitosis when the Par protein aPKC accumulates on the cortex.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Apical actomyosin flows drive the coalescence of aPKC into an apical cap.
source: Apical actomyosin flows drive the coalescence of aPKC into an apical cap that depolarizes in anaphase when the flow reverses direction.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by imaging data in Figure 2 and drug treatment experiments in Figure 3.

claim: The aPKC apical cap depolarizes in anaphase when the actomyosin flow reverses direction.
source: Apical actomyosin flows drive the coalescence of aPKC into an apical cap that depolarizes in anaphase when the flow reverses direction.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data showing temporal correlation between flow reversal and aPKC depolarization.

claim: Anaphase flows play a role in specifying daughter cell size asymmetry.
source: Together with the previously characterized role of anaphase flows in specifying daughter cell size asymmetry, our results indicate that multiple phases of cortical actomyosin dynamics regulate asymmetric cell division.
evidence: This is referenced as previously characterized, indicating it is established knowledge from prior studies.

claim: Multiple phases of cortical actomyosin dynamics regulate asymmetric cell division.
source: Together with the previously characterized role of anaphase flows in specifying daughter cell size asymmetry, our results indicate that multiple phases of cortical actomyosin dynamics regulate asymmetric cell division.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current study's findings combined with prior knowledge.

claim: The Par complex polarizes animal cells by excluding specific factors from the Par cortical domain.
source: The Par complex polarizes animal cells by excluding specific factors from the Par cortical domain (Lang and Munro, 2017; Venkei and Yamashita, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In Drosophila neuroblasts, the Par domain forms at the apical cortex during mitosis where it prevents the accumulation of neuronal fate determinants.
source: In Drosophila neuroblasts, for example, the Par domain forms at the apical cortex during mitosis where it prevents the accumulation of neuronal fate determinants, effectively restricting them to the basal cortex.
evidence: This is established knowledge about neuroblast polarity.

claim: The Par domain effectively restricts neuronal fate determinants to the basal cortex.
source: In Drosophila neuroblasts, for example, the Par domain forms at the apical cortex during mitosis where it prevents the accumulation of neuronal fate determinants, effectively restricting them to the basal cortex.
evidence: This is established knowledge about neuroblast polarity.

claim: Cortical domains are bisected by the cleavage furrow leading to fate determinant segregation into the basal daughter cell.
source: The resulting cortical domains are bisected by the cleavage furrow leading to fate determinant segregation into the basal daughter cell where they promote differentiation (Homem and Knoblich, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Fate determinants promote differentiation in the basal daughter cell.
source: The resulting cortical domains are bisected by the cleavage furrow leading to fate determinant segregation into the basal daughter cell where they promote differentiation (Homem and Knoblich, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Apical Par polarization in the neuroblast is a multistep process in which the complex is initially targeted to the apical hemisphere early in mitosis where it forms a discontinuous meshwork.
source: It was recently discovered that apical Par polarization in the neuroblast is a multistep process in which the complex is initially targeted to the apical hemisphere early in mitosis where it forms a discontinuous meshwork (Kono et al., 2019; Oon and Prehoda, 2019).
evidence: This is recent knowledge supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Cortical Par proteins move along the cortex toward the apical pole, ultimately leading to formation of an apical cap that is maintained until shortly after anaphase onset.
source: Cortical Par proteins then move along the cortex toward the apical pole, ultimately leading to formation of an apical cap that is maintained until shortly after anaphase onset (Oon and Prehoda, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: An intact actin cytoskeleton is required for the movements that polarize Par proteins to the neuroblast apical cortex.
source: An intact actin cytoskeleton is required for the movements that polarize Par proteins to the neuroblast apical cortex, but its role in the polarization process has been unclear.
evidence: This is established knowledge that serves as background for the study.

claim: Depolymerization of F-actin causes apical aPKC to spread to the basal cortex.
source: Depolymerization of F-actin causes apical aPKC to spread to the basal cortex (Hannaford et al., 2018; Oon and Prehoda, 2019), prevents aPKC coalescence, and induces disassembly of the apical aPKC cap (Oon and Prehoda, 2019), suggesting that actin filaments are important for both apical polarity initiation and its maintenance.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Depolymerization of F-actin prevents aPKC coalescence.
source: Depolymerization of F-actin causes apical aPKC to spread to the basal cortex (Hannaford et al., 2018; Oon and Prehoda, 2019), prevents aPKC coalescence, and induces disassembly of the apical aPKC cap (Oon and Prehoda, 2019), suggesting that actin filaments are important for both apical polarity initiation and its maintenance.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Depolymerization of F-actin induces disassembly of the apical aPKC cap.
source: Depolymerization of F-actin causes apical aPKC to spread to the basal cortex (Hannaford et al., 2018; Oon and Prehoda, 2019), prevents aPKC coalescence, and induces disassembly of the apical aPKC cap (Oon and Prehoda, 2019), suggesting that actin filaments are important for both apical polarity initiation and its maintenance.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Actin filaments are important for both apical polarity initiation and its maintenance.
source: Depolymerization of F-actin causes apical aPKC to spread to the basal cortex (Hannaford et al., 2018; Oon and Prehoda, 2019), prevents aPKC coalescence, and induces disassembly of the apical aPKC cap (Oon and Prehoda, 2019), suggesting that actin filaments are important for both apical polarity initiation and its maintenance.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations cited.

claim: Actomyosin plays a central role in generating the anterior Par cortical domain in the C. elegans zygote.
source: How the actin cytoskeleton participates in polarizing the Par complex in neuroblasts has been unclear, but actomyosin plays a central role in generating the anterior Par cortical domain in the C. elegans zygote.
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans that provides context for the neuroblast study.

claim: In C. elegans zygote, contractions oriented toward the anterior pole transport the Par complex from an evenly distributed state.
source: Contractions oriented toward the anterior pole transport the Par complex from an evenly distributed state (Illukkumbura et al., 2020; Lang and Munro, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies on C. elegans.

claim: In C. elegans zygote, bulk transport is mediated by advective flows generated by highly dynamic, transient actomyosin accumulations on the cell cortex.
source: Bulk transport is mediated by advective flows generated by highly dynamic, transient actomyosin accumulations on the cell cortex (Goehring et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on C. elegans.

claim: No apically directed cortical actomyosin dynamics have been observed during the neuroblast polarization process, despite extensive examination.
source: While cortical movements of actomyosin drive formation of the Par domain in the worm zygote and F-actin is required for neuroblast apical Par polarity, no apically directed cortical actomyosin dynamics have been observed during the neuroblast polarization process, despite extensive examination (Barros et al., 2003; Cabernard et al., 2010; Connell et al., 2011; Koe et al., 2018; Roth et al., 2015; Roubinet et al., 2017; Tsankova et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple prior studies that did not observe these dynamics.

claim: Both F-actin and myosin II have been reported to be cytoplasmic or uniformly cortical in interphase, and apically enriched at metaphase.
source: Instead, both F-actin and myosin II have been reported to be cytoplasmic or uniformly cortical in interphase, and apically enriched at metaphase (Barros et al., 2003; Koe et al., 2018; Tsankova et al., 2017), before undergoing cortical flows toward the cleavage furrow that are important for cell size asymmetry (Cabernard et al., 2010; Connell et al., 2011; Roubinet et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: F-actin and myosin II undergo cortical flows toward the cleavage furrow that are important for cell size asymmetry.
source: Instead, both F-actin and myosin II have been reported to be cytoplasmic or uniformly cortical in interphase, and apically enriched at metaphase (Barros et al., 2003; Koe et al., 2018; Tsankova et al., 2017), before undergoing cortical flows toward the cleavage furrow that are important for cell size asymmetry (Cabernard et al., 2010; Connell et al., 2011; Roubinet et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The current model for neuroblast actomyosin dynamics is primarily based on the analysis of fixed cells or by imaging a small number of medial sections in live imaging experiments.
source: The current model for neuroblast actomyosin dynamics is primarily based on the analysis of fixed cells or by imaging a small number of medial sections in live imaging experiments and we recently found that rapid imaging of the full neuroblast volume can reveal dynamic phases of movement that are not detected with other methods (LaFoya and Prehoda, 2021; Oon and Prehoda, 2019).
evidence: This is a characterization of prior methods and their limitations, supported by citations.

claim: Rapid imaging of the full neuroblast volume can reveal dynamic phases of movement that are not detected with other methods.
source: The current model for neuroblast actomyosin dynamics is primarily based on the analysis of fixed cells or by imaging a small number of medial sections in live imaging experiments and we recently found that rapid imaging of the full neuroblast volume can reveal dynamic phases of movement that are not detected with other methods (LaFoya and Prehoda, 2021; Oon and Prehoda, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent work by the authors.

claim: The interphase neuroblast cortex contains patches of concentrated actin, highly dynamic pulsatile waves that travel across the entire width of the cell, and areas with little to no detectable actin.
source: The interphase neuroblast cortex was a mixture of patches of concentrated actin, highly dynamic pulsatile waves that traveled across the entire width of the cell, and areas with little to no detectable actin (Figure 1 and Video 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from imaging data shown in Figure 1 and Video 1.

claim: Pulsatile movements consist of irregular patches of actin forming on the cortex and rapidly moving across the surface before disappearing.
source: Pulsatile movements consisted of irregular patches of actin forming on the cortex and rapidly moving across the surface before disappearing (Figure 1A and E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from imaging data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Concentrated actin patches were relatively static, but sometimes changed size over the course of several minutes.
source: Concentrated actin patches were relatively static, but sometimes changed size over the course of several minutes.
evidence: This is a direct observation from imaging data.

claim: Static patches were mostly unaffected by the pulsatile waves that occasionally passed over them.
source: Static patches were mostly unaffected by the pulsatile waves that occasionally passed over them (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from imaging data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Pulses were sporadic in early interphase but became more regular near mitosis, with a new pulse appearing immediately following the completion of the prior one.
source: Pulses were sporadic in early interphase but became more regular near mitosis, with a new pulse appearing immediately following the completion of the prior one (Figure 1E and Video 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from imaging data shown in Figure 1E and Video 1.

claim: The direction of the pulses during interphase was highly variable, but often along the cell's equator (i.e. orthogonal to the polarity/division axis).
source: The direction of the pulses during interphase was highly variable, but often along the cell's equator (i.e. orthogonal to the polarity/division axis).
evidence: This is a direct observation from imaging data.

claim: Interphase pulses were correlated with cellular scale morphological deformations in which areas of low actin signal were displaced away from the cell center while the cortex containing the actin pulse was compressed toward the center of the cell.
source: Interphase pulses were correlated with cellular scale morphological deformations in which these areas of low actin signal were displaced away from the cell center while the cortex containing the actin pulse was compressed toward the center of the cell (Figure 1D and Video 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from imaging data shown in Figure 1D and Video 1.

claim: Near nuclear envelope breakdown (NEB), the static cortical actin patches began disappearing from the cortex while dynamic cortical actin reoriented toward the apical pole.
source: Near nuclear envelope breakdown (NEB), the static cortical actin patches began disappearing from the cortex while dynamic cortical actin reoriented toward the apical pole (Figure 1 and Video 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from imaging data shown in Figure 1 and Video 1.

claim: The apically directed cortical actin dynamics that began near NEB were highly regular and were apically-directed.
source: In contrast to the sporadic and relatively unoriented interphase pulses observed earlier in the cell cycle, the apically directed cortical actin dynamics that began near NEB were highly regular and were apically-directed (Figure 1E and Video 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from imaging data shown in Figure 1E and Video 1.

claim: The phase of cortical actin dynamics that begins near NEB continues until anaphase.
source: This phase of cortical actin dynamics continued until anaphase–consistent with previous descriptions of actin accumulation at the apical cortex throughout metaphase (Barros et al., 2003; Tsankova et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a direct observation from imaging data, consistent with prior studies cited.

claim: Actin was more evenly-distributed following the transition to mitosis compared to interphase.
source: Additionally, while the interphase cortex had areas with very little actin, actin was more evenly-distributed following the transition, as was apparent in medial sections (e.g. comparing –15:00 and 3:00 in Figure 1D and Video 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from imaging data shown in Figure 1D and Video 1.

claim: Shortly after anaphase onset, the apically directed cortical actin movements rapidly reversed direction such that the F-actin that had accumulated in the apical hemisphere began to move basally toward the emerging cleavage furrow.
source: Another transition in cortical actin dynamics occurred shortly after anaphase onset when the apically directed cortical actin movements rapidly reversed direction such that the F-actin that had accumulated in the apical hemisphere began to move basally toward the emerging cleavage furrow (Figure 1E and Video 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from imaging data shown in Figure 1E and Video 1.

claim: The basally directed phase of movement that begins shortly after anaphase onset includes both actin and myosin II.
source: The basally directed phase of movement that begins shortly after anaphase onset and includes both actin and myosin II was reported previously (Barros et al., 2003; Roubinet et al., 2017; Tsankova et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Par polarity proteins undergo complex cortical dynamics during neuroblast asymmetric cell division.
source: Previously, we showed that Par polarity proteins undergo complex cortical dynamics during neuroblast asymmetric cell division and that polarity cycle movements require an intact actin cytoskeleton (Oon and Prehoda, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Polarity cycle movements require an intact actin cytoskeleton.
source: Previously, we showed that Par polarity proteins undergo complex cortical dynamics during neuroblast asymmetric cell division and that polarity cycle movements require an intact actin cytoskeleton (Oon and Prehoda, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The cortical actin cytoskeleton is highly dynamic at points in the cell cycle when Par proteins undergo coordinated cortical movement.
source: Here, we have found that the cortical actin cytoskeleton is also highly dynamic at points in the cell cycle when Par proteins undergo coordinated cortical movement (Figure 1 and Video 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study supported by imaging data in Figure 1 and Video 1.

claim: The transitions in cortical actin dynamic phases occur when similar transitions take place in the polarity cycle.
source: Furthermore, the transitions in cortical actin dynamic phases appeared to occur when similar transitions take place in the polarity cycle.
evidence: This is an observation inferred from the temporal correlation of events.

claim: Apical targeting of aPKC begins approximately ten minutes before NEB, when small, discontinuous aPKC foci begin to appear.
source: Apical targeting of aPKC began approximately ten minutes before NEB, when small, discontinuous aPKC foci began to appear, as previously reported (Oon and Prehoda, 2019).
evidence: This is an observation from the current study consistent with prior work cited.

claim: The interphase pulses of actin have no noticeable effect on aPKC enrichments.
source: The interphase pulses of actin had no noticeable effect on these aPKC enrichments, suggesting that at this stage of the cell cycle, cortical actin dynamics are not coupled to aPKC movement (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from imaging data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: At the interphase stage of the cell cycle, cortical actin dynamics are not coupled to aPKC movement.
source: The interphase pulses of actin had no noticeable effect on these aPKC enrichments, suggesting that at this stage of the cell cycle, cortical actin dynamics are not coupled to aPKC movement (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that actin pulses do not affect aPKC enrichments.

claim: Cortical actin and aPKC movements are highly correlated beginning in early mitosis.
source: While cortical actin and aPKC did not appear to be coupled during interphase, the two protein's movements were highly correlated beginning in early mitosis (Figure 2 and Video 2).
evidence: This is a direct observation from imaging data shown in Figure 2 and Video 2.

claim: When cortical actin begins flowing apically, the sparsely distributed aPKC patches that had accumulated on the cortex also begin moving toward the apical pole.
source: When cortical actin began flowing apically, the sparsely distributed aPKC patches that had accumulated on the cortex also began moving toward the apical pole.
evidence: This is a direct observation from imaging data.

claim: The transition to apically directed movement is nearly simultaneous for both actin and aPKC.
source: The transition to apically directed movement was nearly simultaneous for both proteins, although actin's apical movement began slightly before aPKC's (actin: 1.9 ± 1.0 min prior to NEB; aPKC: 1.3 ± 1.1 min; n = 13 neuroblasts with movies in Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements from imaging data.

claim: Actin's apical movement begins slightly before aPKC's (actin: 1.9 ± 1.0 min prior to NEB; aPKC: 1.3 ± 1.1 min; n = 13 neuroblasts).
source: The transition to apically directed movement was nearly simultaneous for both proteins, although actin's apical movement began slightly before aPKC's (actin: 1.9 ± 1.0 min prior to NEB; aPKC: 1.3 ± 1.1 min; n = 13 neuroblasts with movies in Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements from imaging data.

claim: While aPKC and actin both move toward the apical cortex, actin dynamics occur over the entire cortex whereas aPKC movements are limited to the apical hemisphere.
source: Furthermore, while aPKC and actin both moved toward the apical cortex, actin dynamics occurred over the entire cortex whereas aPKC movements were limited to the apical hemisphere consistent with its specific targeting to this area (Figure 2 and Video 2).
evidence: This is a direct observation from imaging data shown in Figure 2 and Video 2.

claim: Once aPKC is collected near the pole into an apical cap, it appears to be static while cortical actin continues flowing apically.
source: Interestingly, however, once aPKC was collected near the pole into an apical cap, it appeared to be static while cortical actin continued flowing apically.
evidence: This is a direct observation from imaging data.

claim: The phase of dynamic, apically directed actin with an apparently static aPKC apical cap continues for several minutes.
source: This phase of dynamic, apically directed actin with an apparently static aPKC apical cap continued for several minutes (e.g. until approximately 7:10 in Video 2).
evidence: This is a direct observation from imaging data shown in Video 2.

claim: Actin and aPKC movements reverse simultaneously, moving toward the basal pole and the emerging cleavage furrow.
source: At this point actin and aPKC movements reversed, moving simultaneously toward the basal pole and the emerging cleavage furrow (Figure 2 and Video 2).
evidence: This is a direct observation from imaging data shown in Figure 2 and Video 2.

claim: Cortical actin and aPKC dynamics become highly correlated after interphase actin pulses transition to sustained, apically directed movements.
source: We conclude that cortical actin and aPKC dynamics become highly correlated after interphase actin pulses transition to sustained, apically directed movements.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the imaging observations.

claim: Depolymerization of actin with LatrunculinA (LatA) inhibits aPKC's apically directed cortical movements.
source: The correlation between actin and aPKC dynamics is consistent with our previous finding that depolymerization of actin with LatrunculinA (LatA) inhibits aPKC's apically directed cortical movements (Oon and Prehoda, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Low doses of Cytochalasin D (CytoD) inhibit actin dynamics but maintain cortical structure.
source: We further examined the relationship between F-actin dynamics and aPKC using low doses of Cytochalasin D (CytoD) that inhibit actin dynamics but maintain cortical structure (An et al., 2017; Mason et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The apically directed movements of actin during early mitosis are inhibited by CytoD with the cortex rapidly becoming relatively static.
source: The apically directed movements of actin during early mitosis were inhibited by CytoD with the cortex rapidly becoming relatively static (Figure 3A and A' and Figure 3—video 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from drug treatment experiments shown in Figure 3A and A' and Figure 3—video 1.

claim: The loss of actin dynamics is immediately followed by cessation of apically directed aPKC movement such that it fails to form an apical cap.
source: The loss of actin dynamics was immediately followed by cessation of apically directed aPKC movement such that it failed to form an apical cap (n = 11; neuroblasts shown in Figure 3—video 2).
evidence: This is a direct observation from drug treatment experiments shown in Figure 3—video 2.

claim: Both LatA and CytoD inhibit aPKC coalescence into an apical cap.
source: While both LatA and CytoD inhibited aPKC coalescence into an apical cap, we noticed that aPKC was maintained in the apical hemisphere for a longer period in CytoD-treated neuroblasts (Figure 3B–D, Figure 3—video 3, Figure 3—video 4, and neuroblasts used for measurements in Figure 3—video 5).
evidence: This is a direct observation from drug treatment experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: aPKC is maintained in the apical hemisphere for a longer period in CytoD-treated neuroblasts compared to LatA-treated neuroblasts.
source: While both LatA and CytoD inhibited aPKC coalescence into an apical cap, we noticed that aPKC was maintained in the apical hemisphere for a longer period in CytoD-treated neuroblasts (Figure 3B–D, Figure 3—video 3, Figure 3—video 4, and neuroblasts used for measurements in Figure 3—video 5).
evidence: This is a direct observation from drug treatment experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Some localized enrichments of aPKC remain in the apical hemisphere in neuroblasts treated with either LatA or CytoD, possibly due to their association with localized membrane enrichments.
source: Some localized enrichments remained in the apical hemisphere in neuroblasts treated with either drug, possibly due to their association with localized membrane enrichments, as recently reported (LaFoya and Prehoda, 2021).
evidence: This is an observation with a speculative explanation supported by citation.

claim: aPKC signal enters the basal hemisphere more rapidly in LatA- versus CytoD-treated neuroblasts.
source: However, aPKC signal entered the basal hemisphere more rapidly in LatA- versus CytoD-treated neuroblasts (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from drug treatment experiments shown in Figure 3D.

claim: aPKC is better maintained in its polarized state when the cortical actin cytoskeleton remains intact (CytoD) compared to when it is completely depolymerized (LatA).
source: Thus, aPKC appears to be better maintained in its polarized state when the cortical actin cytoskeleton remains intact (CytoD) compared to when it is completely depolymerized (LatA).
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the drug treatment experiments.

claim: The cortical dynamics that drive the formation of the aPKC apical cap require the apically directed phase of actin dynamics that occurs during late prophase and metaphase.
source: We conclude that the cortical dynamics that drive the formation of the aPKC apical cap require the apically directed phase of actin dynamics that occurs during late prophase and metaphase.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the drug treatment experiments.

claim: Cortical actin structure may prolong the aPKC polarized state by slowing its diffusion into the basal hemisphere.
source: Furthermore, cortical actin structure may prolong the aPKC polarized state by slowing its diffusion into the basal hemisphere.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed difference between LatA and CytoD treatments.

claim: For each phase of actin dynamics, myosin II is localized to the cortex in a similar pattern.
source: For each phase of actin dynamics, we found that myosin II is localized to the cortex in a similar pattern (Figure 4 and Video 3), including during the apically directed continuous movements that polarize aPKC.
evidence: This is a direct observation from imaging data shown in Figure 4 and Video 3.

claim: Myosin II is localized to the cortex during the apically directed continuous movements that polarize aPKC.
source: For each phase of actin dynamics, we found that myosin II is localized to the cortex in a similar pattern (Figure 4 and Video 3), including during the apically directed continuous movements that polarize aPKC.
evidence: This is a direct observation from imaging data shown in Figure 4 and Video 3.

claim: The localization between actin and myosin II is not absolute and there are often large cortical regions where the two do not colocalize in addition to the region where they overlap.
source: Interestingly, however, the localization between the two was not absolute and there were often large cortical regions where the two did not colocalize in addition to the region where they overlapped (Figure 4 and Video 3).
evidence: This is a direct observation from imaging data shown in Figure 4 and Video 3.

claim: A similar pattern of overlapping cortical actin and myosin II localization has been reported in the polarizing worm zygote.
source: A similar pattern of overlapping cortical actin and myosin II localization has been reported in the polarizing worm zygote (Reymann et al., 2016; Michaux et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies on C. elegans.

claim: The phases of cortical actin dynamics that occur during neuroblast asymmetric cell division include both actin and myosin II.
source: Given the similarities in behavior of actin and myosin II, we conclude that the phases of cortical actin dynamics that occur during neuroblast asymmetric cell division include both actin and myosin II.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the imaging observations of actin and myosin II.

claim: During interphase when aPKC is cytoplasmic, actomyosin pulsatile contractions are predominantly equatorial.
source: During interphase when aPKC is cytoplasmic, actomyosin pulsatile contractions are predominantly equatorial.
evidence: This is shown in the summary diagram in Figure 5 and is based on the imaging data.

claim: During apical polarity initiation in prophase and shortly before when discrete aPKC cortical patches begin to coalesce, actomyosin transitions to more continuous movements directed toward the apical cortex.
source: During apical polarity initiation in prophase and shortly before when discrete aPKC cortical patches begin to coalesce, actomyosin transitions to more continuous movements directed toward the apical cortex.
evidence: This is shown in the summary diagram in Figure 5 and is based on the imaging data.

claim: At anaphase apical actomyosin is cleared as it flows toward the cleavage furrow while the aPKC cap is disassembled.
source: At anaphase apical actomyosin is cleared as it flows toward the cleavage furrow while the aPKC cap is disassembled.
evidence: This is shown in the summary diagram in Figure 5 and is based on the imaging data.

claim: Myosin II pulses have been observed in delaminating neuroblasts from the Drosophila embryonic neuroectoderm.
source: While cortical actomyosin dynamics had not been reported during neuroblast polarization, myosin II pulses have been observed in delaminating neuroblasts from the Drosophila embryonic neuroectoderm (An et al., 2017; Simões et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Apically directed movements of actomyosin are consistent with the requirement for F-actin in the coalescence of discrete aPKC patches into an apical cap.
source: First, apically directed movements of actomyosin are consistent with the requirement for F-actin in the coalescence of discrete aPKC patches into an apical cap (Figure 3; Oon and Prehoda, 2019).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the observed actomyosin movements to the known requirement for F-actin.

claim: In the worm zygote, pulsatile contractions generate bulk cortical flows (i.e. advection) that lead to non-specific transport of cortically localized components.
source: In the worm zygote, pulsatile contractions generate bulk cortical flows (i.e. advection) that lead to non-specific transport of cortically localized components (Goehring et al., 2011; Illukkumbura et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies on C. elegans.

claim: Whether the cortical motions of polarity proteins that occur during the neuroblast polarity cycle are driven by advection requires further study.
source: Whether the cortical motions of polarity proteins that occur during the neuroblast polarity cycle are also driven by advection will require further study.
evidence: This is a statement acknowledging the need for future investigation.

claim: The more rapid depolarization of aPKC in LatA- compared to CytoD-treated neuroblasts is consistent with a potentially passive role for the actin cytoskeleton in polarity maintenance.
source: The more rapid depolarization of aPKC in Lat- compared to CytoD-treated neuroblasts (Figure 3B–D), is also consistent with a potentially passive role for the actin cytoskeleton in polarity maintenance.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the drug treatment experiments.

claim: Complete loss of the cortical actin cytoskeleton (LatA) leads to more rapid entry of aPKC into the basal neuroblast membrane compared to when cortical actin dynamics is inhibited but the structure maintained (CytoD).
source: Complete loss of the cortical actin cytoskeleton (LatA; Figure 3B) leads to more rapid entry of aPKC into the basal neuroblast membrane compared to when cortical actin dynamics is inhibited but the structure maintained (CytoD; Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from drug treatment experiments shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: The difference in aPKC depolarization between LatA and CytoD treatment could arise from an increase in cortical diffusion constant when the cortical actin mesh is removed.
source: The difference could arise simply from an increase in cortical diffusion constant when the cortical actin mesh is removed.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed difference.

claim: The actin cytoskeleton participates in Par polarity via at least two mechanisms: by generating non-diffusive movements of polarity proteins through actomyosin-generated cortical flows, and by maintaining the polarized state by slowing the rate of diffusion.
source: In this case, the actin cytoskeleton would participate in Par polarity via at least two mechanisms: by generating non-diffusive movements of polarity proteins through actomyosin-generated cortical flows (Figures 2 and 3), and by maintaining the polarized state by slowing the rate of diffusion (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations and drug treatments.

claim: A neuroblast membrane polarity cycle was recently discovered and found to require the actin cytoskeleton.
source: While we have examined the relationship between actomyosin dynamics and cortical protein polarity, we note that a neuroblast membrane polarity cycle was recently discovered and found to require the actin cytoskeleton (LaFoya and Prehoda, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent work by the authors.

claim: The mechanical phases of the membrane polarity cycle may be related to the phases of cortical actomyosin dynamics reported in this study.
source: The mechanical phases of the membrane polarity cycle may be related to the phases of cortical actomyosin dynamics we report here.
evidence: This is a speculative connection between the current findings and prior work.

claim: Optical sections through the entire neuroblast volume (~40 0.5 µm sections) were collected at 10 s intervals beginning in interphase and through at least one mitosis.
source: To follow cortical actin dynamics across full asymmetric division cycles, we collected optical sections through the entire neuroblast volume (~40 0.5 µm sections) at 10 s intervals beginning in interphase and through at least one mitosis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the imaging methodology used in the study.

claim: Maximum intensity projections constructed from imaging data revealed localized actin enrichments on the cortex, some of which were highly dynamic.
source: Maximum intensity projections constructed from these data revealed localized actin enrichments on the cortex, some of which were highly dynamic (Figure 1 and Video 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from imaging data shown in Figure 1 and Video 1.

claim: Three discrete phases of cortical actin dynamics precede the previously characterized basally directed flows that occur in late anaphase.
source: We observed three discrete phases of cortical actin dynamics that preceded the previously characterized basally directed flows that occur in late anaphase (Roubinet et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, with the late anaphase flows supported by citation.

claim: The transition to apically directed cortical actin movements occurs when cortical actin begins flowing apically near nuclear envelope breakdown.
source: Near nuclear envelope breakdown (NEB), the static cortical actin patches began disappearing from the cortex while dynamic cortical actin reoriented toward the apical pole (Figure 1 and Video 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the description of events occurring near NEB.

claim: Cortical actomyosin dynamics are force-generating processes.
source: The morphological changes in interphase cells (Figure 1D and Video 1) and cortical aPKC movements that were correlated with cortical actin dynamics in early mitosis (Figure 2 and Video 2), are consistent with a force generating process.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed morphological changes and protein movements.

claim: Contractile forces are generated by the combined activity of F-actin and myosin II (i.e. actomyosin).
source: While actin can generate force directly through polymerization, contractile forces are generated by the combined activity of F-actin and myosin II (i.e. actomyosin), and cortical pulsatile contractions of actomyosin have been observed in many other systems (Vicker, 2000; Munro et al., 2004; Michaux et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Cortical pulsatile contractions of actomyosin have been observed in many other systems.
source: While actin can generate force directly through polymerization, contractile forces are generated by the combined activity of F-actin and myosin II (i.e. actomyosin), and cortical pulsatile contractions of actomyosin have been observed in many other systems (Vicker, 2000; Munro et al., 2004; Michaux et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The localization of myosin II in neuroblasts has been described as uniformly cortical or cytoplasmic in interphase and before metaphase in mitosis.
source: The localization of myosin II in neuroblasts has been described as uniformly cortical or cytoplasmic in interphase and before metaphase in mitosis (Barros et al., 2003; Tsankova et al., 2017; Koe et al., 2018).
evidence: This is prior knowledge supported by citations.
